idiom_name: Money struct over shopspring/decimal plus an ISO 4217 code
implementation_notes: Go has no decimal primitive: math/big.Rat is exact but the decimal library's own guidance argues it is the wrong tool for money, because rationals produce repeating expansions that must be truncated anyway, whereas Decimal prints exactly what it stores. The idiomatic realization is therefore a small Money struct pairing shopspring/decimal with an ISO 4217 code, with Add/Sub/Mul/Div methods that reject currency mismatches, a Split or Allocate helper that assigns the remainder, and sql.Scanner/driver.Valuer plus JSON marshalling that never emits a bare float. Interrogate the library's Div: it requires an explicit precision, and that requirement is exactly where the rounding policy lives.
pitfalls: decimal.Div requires the caller to name the precision; omitting the rounding decision there is the classic Go money bug.
Decimal values are immutable, so every operation allocates - hot loops should reuse or switch to fixed-scale int64 arithmetic.
Marshalling a decimal as a JSON number hands the value to parsers that read it as a double, so the string form belongs on the wire.

variants.name: Int64 minor units with an explicit scale field
variants.idiom_name: Money{Minor int64; Currency string; Scale int32}
variants.implementation_notes: The zero-dependency route stores an int64 count of minor units plus the currency code and its scale, as the integer-based go-money packages do: addition, subtraction and comparison stay exact integer arithmetic, and the value is a comparable struct that is cheap to copy. Division, percentages and conversion then go through helpers that round once with an explicit mode, and allocation hands the remainder out unit by unit. Choose it for zero-allocation paths and small services; choose the decimal route when amounts carry more scale than the currency's minor unit.
pitfalls: int64 overflow wraps silently in Go, so totals near the limit need math.MaxInt64 checks or a wider type.
Carrying the scale means two representations of one currency can differ, so the scale must be normalised at the boundary.
A float64 must never appear anywhere in the pipeline: printing minor units directly also looks like the wrong amount.
